title: Phoenicia
capsule: Phoenicia designates the cluster of maritime city-states — principally Tyre, Sidon, Byblos, and Arwad — that dominated the Levantine coast from roughly 1150 BCE and drove Mediterranean trade and colonization for six centuries, founding Carthage (traditionally 814 BCE) and establishing emporia as far west as Gadir (Cádiz). Each city-state maintained its own hereditary kingship; Tyre under Hiram I (r. c. 969–936 BCE) was the dominant power, supplying timber and craftsmen for Solomon's Temple and expanding commercial networks across Cyprus and the Aegean. Phoenicia came under successive Assyrian, Babylonian, and Achaemenid Persian overlordship from the 9th century onward, with Tyre finally besieged and captured by Alexander the Great in 332 BCE after a seven-month siege. The dataset's terminal date of c. 500 BCE reflects the point at which the cities lost meaningful political autonomy under Persian rule.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The core coastal city-states are well attested in Assyrian annals, Hebrew scriptures, and Greek sources, but mapping Phoenicia as a territorial unit is inherently problematic because it was never a unified polity; extent polygons are necessarily schematic.
